newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan girds for lonely battle to halt yen's slide.
newsitem.headline: Japan girds for lonely battle to halt yen's slide.

text.p: Japan's monetary authorities are ready to step into currency markets and fight a lonely battle to halt the yen's slide, despite conflicting views on intervention among Japanese officials, traders say.
Japanese cabinet minister Kabun Muto said on Friday that any "artificial" attempt to check a further fall in the yen could fail in the present environment of a continuing capital outflow from Japan.

"An artificial attempt to check a further slide by the yen may not yield any result, given that Japan's low interest rates are pushing Japanese capital abroad," said Muto, who is director-general of the Management and Coordination Agency.

He said the Bank of Japan (BOJ) should increase its official discount rate (ODR) by the year-end to stop capital outflows from Japan. Muto said there was nothing wrong with the dollar moving above 125 yen, adding that in terms of purchasing power parity, 150 yen to the dollar would be appropriate.

But a Ministry of Finance official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters soon afterwards: "Muto's remarks regarding the dollar/yen rate do not reflect the official policy of the Japanese government."
He added: "The official view is, as the finance minister (Hiroshi Mitsuzuka) said, that the yen's recent falls are overdone and (the ministry) is concerned about it."
Japan would take decisive measures to deal with excessive moves in the currency markets, he added.
Conflicting views over currency movements among Japanese officials are puzzling foreign exchange traders.
The dollar was at 126 yen in Tokyo on Friday, after hitting a 56-month high of 127.16 yen on Thursday. The yen has slid 58 percent from its high of 79.75 yen to the dollar in April 1995.
Still, traders in Tokyo expect the Bank of Japan to sell dollars for yen if there is another rise, in a bid to clarify its stance and back up the strong words with real action.
But they said concerted action by other central banks to stem the dollar's rise was unlikely.

"The Bank of Japan is set for an imminent action (dollar-selling intervention), but they will have to do it alone," said Takeshi Hanai, executive manager of the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd's International Treasury Department.
On Thursday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said he shared Japan's concern about the yen's recent fall, but also reiterated that a strong dollar is in the U.S.'s interests.
Rubin's statement suggested that Washington supports the Bank of Japan's independent attempt to check a further dollar rally, but is reluctant to use its own money, traders said.

"The only problem would be that the speed of the yen's falls could fuel friction with United States over trade issues. So single-handed intervention is feasible," said Takuma Kurosawa, chief manager at Mitsubishi Trust and Banking.

"While the U.S. keeps up a strong dollar policy for the sake of its financial markets, it's necessary for Japan to demonstrate that it is coping with the yen's falls to soothe worries of U.S. exporters," he added.

The United States is averse to a stronger yen because of expectations that U.S. interest rates will be raised once if not more times this year, which would lead to dollar buying, said John Reedyk, head of international sales at ANZ Bank, Melbourne.
"They are happy to have the dollar down a little bit before then to absorb some effects of (U.S.) rate rises," he told Reuters Financial Television.
